runs.text: and a skincare routine involving ice cubes.
my phone has over 11,000 unread emails,
and I talk to myself in the cereal aisle
like I’m giving a TED Talk.
I was deeply loyal to my version of the story. Not because I didn’t know better. I did. But I hadn’t realized just how far I had gone to protect the narrative I built.

I mapped it all out. When someone disrupted it, I felt personally attacked. I was like a castaway with only a soccer ball for company. The island was mine. The story was mine. I used to picture myself like the character from “Cast Away,” alone, speaking to a ball, keeping myself sane in a world no one else could reach.
Here’s the truth. I’ve never actually watched that movie. I didn’t need to. The clips were enough. I saw myself in them. I wasn’t ready to face my own reflection.

I told myself I was looking for truth. But I wasn’t. I was hiding from it. What I really wanted was safety, and my version of events gave me that. Truth was dangerous. It asked for change. And change meant letting go of control.
I had come to rely on the very things I once feared. They became familiar. Predictable.

In my head, the world was peaceful. It looked like a Bob Ross painting or a sitcom from the 90s. Calm, soft, edited. But reality never matched, so I turned away. I chose the island, even when it hurt.

I started to wonder if I’d ever let go of the story, I told myself. Whether I’d ever stop defending the fiction and confront what was real. Feeling things fully brought change and change often felt like death. Still, I survived it. Barely. But I did.

And here’s what I finally saw. I wasn’t alone. I had people, an army even. Not on the island itself, but just offshore, waiting. I didn’t believe I deserved them, but they stayed anyway. Out of love. Out of care. Even through chaos.

I’ve always been drawn to the flawed. The cracked. The messy. Because they were real. They spoke my language. The broken have always been my people. I believe everyone is made of both scars and light. We carry both.

I have power. Both healing and destructive. And they come from the same source. What matters is how I use them. The universe doesn’t sort intention into right and wrong. It just responds. A devil can make a hell. A hurting heart can make a worse one. But that same heart can also build something safe.
Light and dark both live in me. They always have.
My struggle was never about loving others. It was about letting anyone get close enough to love me. I lived on an island, speaking to a ball, pretending no one else could hear.
Lately I’ve been wondering. Maybe it’s time I give that ball a name?
She knows four kinds of silence,
the mezcal will take the blame.
